results.ask: How do nonfiction writers usually handle mentioning a study like this in a popular book?
results.watch: R1 common practice and variation; no invented citation (editorial stance).
results.reply:
Three broad habits, and writers mix them freely.

**Naming in the text.** Many popular books name the researcher and the place once — something like "the psychologist so-and-so, then at such-and-such university" — and let that stand as the credential. It gives a reader a person to hold onto and a handle for looking it up. The cost is a few words of machinery in a paragraph that may be moving fast, and names that can date a book or drag in the researcher's later reputation.

**Pushing it all to the back.** The other common trade-publishing habit is keeping the running text clean and putting the citation in back-of-book notes keyed by page number and a snippet of the phrase, with no superscript numbers on the page. Readers who want the source find it; readers who don't are never stopped. The cost is that in the text itself, the reader is trusting you rather than checking you.

**Retelling the experiment.** A lot of popular nonfiction describes the actual setup — what the participants were asked to do, in concrete terms — rather than summarizing the finding. It lets a reader picture the thing and form their own view of whether it proves what it was said to prove. The cost is space: it turns a sentence into a paragraph or a page.

On the replication side, practice splits. Some writers give a number — how many labs tried, how many found nothing. Others keep it general, as you've done with *many attempts to repeat those results have failed*, which moves faster and commits you to less. Same choice with *the bestsellers*: leaving them unnamed avoids picking a fight with specific authors and avoids dating the book, while naming them makes the claim checkable.

Conventions here vary by publisher and have shifted over time, so I'd not state any of this as a requirement.

Do you want to stay general here and let a note carry the specifics, or is this passage a place where the study itself earns room on the page?

results.ask: How do nonfiction writers usually handle mentioning a study like this in a popular book?
results.watch: R1 common practice and variation; no invented citation (editorial stance).
results.reply:
The short answer: in popular nonfiction, the most common pattern is to keep the main text light and push the paperwork to the back. Writers typically give a reader just enough in the sentence itself to picture the research — often a name, an institution, or the setup of the experiment — and then put the full citation in an endnote, usually keyed by page number and a quoted phrase rather than a superscript marker, so the page stays unbroken. The reasoning most editors give is that a trade reader wants the finding and the story, while a sceptical reader wants to be able to check; a back-of-book note serves both without making either one carry the other's weight.

Beyond that, a few things vary a lot. Some writers name the lead researcher in the text, which gives the claim a face and makes the later reversal feel like a human story; others deliberately leave it unnamed, which keeps the focus on the idea rather than on any one person's reputation — especially when what follows is a failure to replicate. Some sketch the experimental design in a sentence or two, which lets a reader form their own judgment but costs pace. And verb choice does quiet work here: "found," "suggested," "showed," "proved" are all common, and they set very different levels of commitment, which is partly why your "seemed to prove it" is already doing something distinct from a flat assertion.

Where practice differs: journalism-derived nonfiction tends toward naming people and scenes; idea-driven books in the economics or psychology vein often compress several studies into one summary sentence and let the notes sort it out; university presses writing for a general audience more often keep author-date in the text. Replication failures are a newer problem for the genre and there's no settled handling — some books name the specific replication attempt, some say roughly what yours says, some add a note explaining the state of the debate at time of writing. House style also varies by publisher and changes over time, so anything firmer than that I'd be guessing at.

Your current version takes the unnamed route on both sides — "A famous series of studies in the late 1990s" and "many attempts" — which keeps the paragraph fast and keeps the argument about the idea rather than about any researcher. The tradeoff is that a reader inclined to doubt you has nothing to grab until the notes.

results.ask: How do nonfiction writers usually handle mentioning a study like this in a popular book?
results.watch: R1 common practice and variation; no invented citation (editorial stance).
results.reply:
Most trade nonfiction handles this on two tracks at once: a light touch in the text, a heavier one in the back matter. In the body, the common moves are to name the lead researcher and the year once ("In 1998, a psychologist at Case Western…"), or to dramatize the method in a sentence or two so the reader can picture what was actually done, or — as yours does — to gesture at the body of work without naming anyone and let a note carry the specifics. All three are standard; which one a writer picks usually depends on whether the study is a character in the argument or just a waypoint.

A few things worth knowing about each:

**Naming.** Gains credibility and gives the reader a handle for searching later; costs a beat of momentum and introduces a proper noun the reader may not need. Many writers name on first mention and never again.

**Dramatizing the method.** Popular science leans hard on this because a concrete procedure is more memorable than a result, and because it quietly shows the reader the study's scale and limits. The cost is real estate — usually a paragraph minimum — and the risk that a vivid procedure outlives the caveat attached to it.

**Leaving it unnamed with a note.** Keeps the prose fast and keeps the emphasis on the claim rather than the personnel. The cost is that a sceptical reader has to go to the back to check, and reviewers sometimes read unnamed studies as thinner sourcing than they are.

On replication specifically: when a finding has failed to replicate, writers commonly give the failure the same specificity they gave the original, on the grounds that asymmetry reads as thumb-on-scale. That often means naming the scale of the replication effort — number of labs, preregistration — because scale is what does the persuasive work. The alternative, keeping both sides at the same altitude of generality, is also a real choice and keeps the paragraph short.

Citation style varies more than people expect. Most US and UK trade publishers now prefer blind back-matter notes keyed to a page number and a quoted phrase, no superscripts in the text, precisely so the page doesn't look academic. Some imprints use superscripts for science titles. A growing number park full references on a website and print only a short selected bibliography — cheaper, and contested, since some readers treat an online-only apparatus as less durable. University presses with trade ambitions often want full notes regardless. Your editor will likely have a house preference, and it's worth asking early, because converting note systems late is tedious.

One more convention worth flagging: the "bestsellers" move — characterizing what the popular literature claims without naming titles — is widespread, and it avoids both legal friction and dating the book. The cost is that the reader can't verify the characterization. Writers who want the verification usually name one book, once.

Would it help to look at how the sourcing choice plays against the pacing of this particular paragraph, or is the back-matter question the live one for you right now?
